en: Jingye Zhijin Lingyan Shanxia Baozang Seng, Wukai, relates:
That which the world calls the "sea of suffering" is so named because the places of suffering are many while the places of joy are few. Although there is joy...
Wherever one dwells, one can never escape suffering. In reality, the world is nothing but a mass of painful circumstances; this is why it is called the "Sea of Suffering.
As for the suffering inherent in painful places, everyone knows it and there is no need to speak further. However, as for the suffering within pleasant places, most people do not realize it;
I shall now briefly explain it. Wealth and honor are what people delight in, yet wealth brings its own anxieties.
The noble have their own noble anxieties. Whatever constitutes anxiety is, by its very nature, suffering.
As for the locus of these anxieties, each family has its own affairs, numbering in the thousands and tens of thousands; it need not be explained in detail.

How much more so for those of great wealth and status—the more they possess, the more evil karma they create, and the easier it becomes to fall into the great realms of rebirth. Once evil karma has been created, in the blink of an eye—
When the retribution for evil arrives, it truly kills one with suffering. Is this not the sea of suffering?
Since you have come to know that the world is such a sea of suffering, why do you not leap out of this sea of suffering to forever leave it behind and attain great peace and happiness?
If you seek peace and happiness, you must certainly practice; if you are willing—
In practicing cultivation, it is necessary to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
If you are willing to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, simply recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha. Having practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, it is necessary to make a vow.
This vow is not to seek favorable conditions in this present life, nor is it to seek them in future lives.
As for the benefits: why is this? It is said that the world is always a sea of suffering; I do not seek any benefit within this sea of suffering.
I seek only that when my breath ceases, I may still recite one phrase: "Namo Amitābha Buddha."
Let him be as he may, bound by the suffering of illness; I shall simply recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
Whatever I eat, whatever I wear, and whatever I use—each and every thing—I cast aside from my concerns. Even the person I hold dear in my heart, I no longer keep in mind;
even my own body I disregard. Let life and death follow their course; I do nothing but recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion. You!
If you can do this, Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss will immediately emit a great radiance that illuminates you.

Your body and mind will then become cool and refreshed, free from all hindrances. Before your eyes, you will naturally behold the Buddha’s light, as if sitting amidst a clear blue sky and bright sunlight.
Continue reciting the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion, further reinforced by the sincerity you have cultivated in your daily life.
At this moment of diligent practice, within a great radiance, you will see with your own eyes a lotus flower made of the seven treasures close at hand;
from afar, you will behold the golden bodies of Amitābha Buddha,
Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who come to welcome and lead you to rebirth in the Western Land.
I have spoken thus to reveal the dharma-gate of the practice of *nien-fo*. Do you believe this most deeply?
If you believe it deeply, then practice accordingly. If there should be any doubt, I shall explain it further for you until it is clear.
People of the world generally can only look after themselves. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having already delivered themselves, observe all sentient beings and vow to deliver them all.
For this reason, they extensively expound the methods of practice; by practicing according to these methods, there is not one who is not delivered.
If sentient beings do not believe in the Buddha-dharma and are unwilling to practice, they lack the karmic affinity with the Buddha; the Buddha will then be unable to deliver them.
If you can believe and practice, it means that in previous lives you possessed roots of goodness and in this life you possess affinity with the Buddha.
Having affinity with the Buddha, when you practice, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will surely protect and assist you. You will then obtain the power of the Buddha.
May they be protected. If one practices with renewed sincerity, there will be no failure.
Generally, those who practice but do not achieve success do so because their recitation of the Buddha’s name lacks sincerity;
or, though they recite the Buddha’s name, they still harbor worldly desires and cannot focus their mind and intention solely on seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land.
This is because one delights in the world of bliss.
For those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, the recitation of the Buddha’s name must be treated as the essential reality.
All worldly affairs and the management of one's household are merely external husks; yet, this essential reality does not obstruct the external husks, nor do the external husks obstruct it.
This is truly essential. One attains the way of mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti).

When opening one's eyes to recite the Buddha’s name, the mind easily becomes distracted; it is better, therefore, to recite with eyes closed. As for the two ears hearing sounds, it is difficult to block them.
Since they cannot be blocked, one must instead borrow something else to employ. How is this method to be applied? When reciting the Buddha’s name, one should...
When this mind is released into a state of empty and lucid clarity, take up the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha. Then, as you recite, you listen;
as you listen, you recite. Let it flow on continuously, winding its way along as a single path. This is the most sublime secret method for reciting the Buddha’s name.
If you practice this for a long time, there will surely come a moment of resonance.

The six-character recitation and the four-character recitation are the same. (To recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" is called the six-character recitation; to simply recite "Amitābha Buddha" is called the four-character recitation.
One may recite while walking or sitting; the more one does, the better. From day until night, if you forget, recite as soon as you remember.
If interrupted by other matters, resume reciting once those affairs are concluded. One may recite either aloud or silently.

Reciting silently without making a sound is the same as reciting aloud; however, one must ensure that every word arises earnestly from the mind and every phrase emerges from the aspiration to be reborn in the Western Land.
Furthermore, there is a method for maintaining mindfulness: even when not reciting the Buddha’s name.
This thought should be constantly kept in mind by Amitābha Buddha (every day at dawn, he rises from his bed).

Pure and pristine, with not a single thought arising, sit until after sunrise. Then, gently descending from the meditation seat, slightly shift your attention; let there be nothing but contemplation on the matters of cultivation. In this way, wisdom is most effectively developed.
The mind is always pure, unmoving and unshakable; this is the place where the power of practice is gained.
As the daily devotions of one who recites the Buddha’s name: recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* once and the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha Dhāraṇī* three times.

Upon finishing the recitation of the Buddha’s name, recite the names of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean ten times each. Recite them thus.
One section of the Dedication Text. Perform three prostrations to Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Ocean;
then complete the Three Refuges. Morning and evening, it is always thus. This constitutes the practice for the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name, being single-minded and without distraction.
If one wishes to recite the mantras of various Mahāyāna sūtras and so forth, it is better to set aside a separate time and establish this as the midday service (*muk-kwa*).
It is not appropriate to intermingle such practices within the primary morning and evening services; for if they are intermingled, one’s practice will lack single-minded concentration.
The *Gao Wang Jing*, the *Fen Zhu Jing*, the *Xiang Shan Juan*, and the *Fo Ji* are all not to be recited; they are not found in the Tripitaka and are therefore not authentic scriptures.

Regarding bamboo-thread lanterns: it is said that after death, they are used for illumination in the underworld (ming-si). This shows a complete disregard for the principles of reciting the Buddha’s name (*nianfo*).
I exhort the people of the world to instead light "Nianfo Lanterns. Once they are fully lit, record their names and count them; it is best to incinerate them before the Buddha.
Since the Buddha’s own light shines upon one another, what need is there for bamboo-thread lamps?
One must master the *Amitābha Sūtra*; the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* should be read constantly.
Aside from one's daily recitations, it is best to set aside a fixed period each day for prostrations.
Standing directly before the Buddha, one should pray with earnest sincerity and single-minded devotion, seeking the Buddha’s compassionate pity and requesting that his light of mercy shine upon me.

Before the Dharma-Buddha, burn incense and, with a sincere heart, join your palms. For every recitation of one syllable, perform one prostration (this should be done with the *vaṃdanā* [homage] gesture). Recite as follows:
Homage to the present Tathāgata of the Sahā world, our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, who possesses great kindness and great compassion.
(Nine prostrations) Homage to the Great Compassionate One of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Teacher who guides and leads us with his great vows and great power.
Amitābha Buddha. (Forty-eight prostrations) Homage to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, to the myriad billions with bodies of purple-gold. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
(Three prostrations)
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, whose body is the wisdom of boundless light in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
(Three prostrations) Homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, who possess bodies of perfected twofold adornment and are as vast as a pure great ocean.
Mahāsattva. (Three prostrations.
Having finished the prostrations, kneel for a long time and, with a sincere mind, join the palms and recite:
"Whatever evil karma I have created in the past, All arises from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion."
Arising from body, speech, and mind, I now seek repentance before the Buddha. May I,
at the time when my life is about to end, Completely eliminate all obstacles,
Behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, And immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
"Though space may come to an end, my vow shall be inexhaustible; may sentient and insentient beings alike realize the Perfect Wisdom.
Having finished this recitation, stand up, perform three prostrations, and withdraw.
The practice I am now expounding takes the recitation of the Buddha's name and the making of vows as its primary focus.
Nevertheless, auxiliary conditions for the path are indispensable. What are these auxiliary conditions? They are: a mind of reverence toward the Triple Gem;

a mind aspiring for transcendence from the world; a mind of weary detachment from entanglements; a mind that understands the retribution of good and evil and gives rise to a sense of awe; and a mind of uprightness.
The sincere mind, the compassionate mind, the mind of liberation, and the mind that does not seek the excellence of one's own path—all these are virtuous dispositions;
they are the causal conditions that assist the Way.
Once one possesses a virtuous mind as an aid to the Path, one must also recognize a corrupt mind in order to prevent it from obstructing the Path.
These include: a mind that lacks faith in the Triple Gem; a mind that acts according to its own arbitrary whims while practicing;
a mind seeking fame and profit; a mind craving worldly pleasures; a mind of anger; a mind of ignorance and delusion; a mind seeking worldly blessings and rewards; and a mind of clever artifice.
A deceitful mind, a biased and crooked mind, a mind of habitual indolence, a mind that refuses to reform its faults, and a mind that considers itself right—all of these are corrupted dispositions.
Even if one practices cultivation, it will be extremely difficult to enter the Way.
The reason for this is that such minds act as obstructions.
To accomplish the task of practice, you must certainly draw near to enlightened teachers and virtuous friends and follow their instructions.

If you do not encounter such teachers and friends, then one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and one essay on the text of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) shall serve as your teachers and friends; however, you must strictly avoid fabricating them yourself.
Among enlightened teachers and virtuous friends, there are both the genuine and the false. If you require teachers and friends, you must seek the genuine ones, for only they can lead you forward.
It leads one into the Way, opens up one's wisdom, perfects one's cultivation, and brings an end to one's birth and death.

Therefore, the kindness of teachers and friends exceeds that of one's parents. If they were false, they would lead one onto wrong paths and suffocate one’s sincere mind for right practice, causing one to achieve nothing at all.
Thus, the distinction between the true and the false is no less than that between heaven and earth.
One must not fail to discern and then draw near [to such a person].
I shall now explain a method for discernment. As for one who is a true, enlightened teacher or a virtuous friend, they may not necessarily be apparent at first sight.
However, there is a certain quality of an enlightened teacher or virtuous friend that I will show you; it is simply this: being level.
It is simply a matter of being plain and real. When it comes to cultivation, one must investigate what you yourself are practicing in a systematic and orderly manner, neither too high nor too low.
Upon hearing this, you will find that your daily practice has been significantly illuminated and developed.

One also observes that it accords with the scriptures in ways that are not apparent. If it were a fabrication, upon first sight it would immediately bear the likeness of a true master or a virtuous friend.
Yet when it comes to discussing cultivation, it will surely overturn what you have practiced daily in a different tune, in order to appear superior.

For example, suppose you have habitually recited a single scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* according to the Buddha’s instructions; [the fabricated teaching] would treat this in a completely different manner.
Regarding the invocation of the Name and the aspiration for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, what is incorrect about it?
Why must you necessarily change the musical mode and establish a different *huatou* (critical phrase)? Do you perhaps surpass Śākyamuni Buddha?

If there were actual errors among practitioners, it would be appropriate to prescribe medicine according to their ailments; if they truly have points that are not yet clear, one should further explain them according to their individual capacities.
The practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is to be employed at the time of death; that which is employed at the time of death must be cultivated during one's ordinary life.
As for practicing during one's ordinary life, it is better while one’s physical strength is robust than when one is aged and infirm.
Therefore, be careful not to be negligent or to defer it to some future day.
Your own practice has not yet reached a state of firm realization, and your understanding of the Buddha-dharma is not yet clear; therefore, you must not easily teach others.
Even if you harbor the intention to be a teacher—claiming it is for the sake of benefiting both yourself and others—I fear nothing but that you will only lead yourself astray and mislead others.
Although a practitioner’s body should not be clung to with craving, it must still be nurtured. When one reaches old age, one should simply gather back all scattered movements within one's practice;
there is no need to make special arrangements for the body because of its aging. If one has a minor illness, take medicine; if one has a major illness, wait for death.
By no means should one strive for recovery from a serious illness; one should simply maintain an upright posture and depart for home.

If at the time of death one encounters a terminal illness and suffers extraordinary agony, one should know that this is the karmic retribution for evil deeds committed throughout successive lifetimes.
At such a moment, one must practice the Buddha-remembrance of "desperate flight" (*wang-ming nianfo*). Amidst a thousand demons and a hundred hardships, my mind shall remain unmoved and unshaken.
There are no difficult matters in the world. It all depends on one’s resolve. Once the resolve is determined, nothing is difficult.
When sailing upon the lakes and seas, one must rely on rowing the oars; traveling a hundred li in a single day is already considered good.
Yet, if one encounters a great following wind, one may travel several hundred li in an instant. Why is it so fast? Heaven assists its power. This is true for all things.

To take rebirth in the Western Pure Land while relying solely on human effort is naturally difficult. If one recites the Buddha’s name with a sincere and earnest heart, the Buddha will surely protect them.

Protection through the Buddha’s power is even superior to divine assistance; therefore, it is not difficult. If one wishes to rely solely on the Buddha’s power while one’s own practice lacks sincerity, one will ultimately fail and end up resenting the Buddha.
One should know that such resentment is misplaced. It is one's own lack of diligence that should be resented.
Likewise, when a person is conceived within a mother’s womb, it is never considered difficult nor is it regarded as extraordinary. Why?
Because everyone has grown accustomed to it and considers it a matter of fact. So too is the rebirth through *nien-fo* in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Lotus-Body Transformation is difficult to perceive and marvelous because one has never been accustomed to seeing it;
yet, how could one know that its actual principle is identical to that of a person being born from a mother’s womb?
One is brought about through emotional attachment, while the other is brought about through faith and aspiration.
When a person recites the Buddha’s name to attain rebirth in the Western Land, they first escape the sea of suffering and leap out of the cycle of the six realms of existence;
after attaining rebirth, they practice until they reach Buddhahood.
The single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is direct and straightforward from beginning to end, without the slightest detour.
Many practitioners achieve success through hardship; look at those who live in comfort—how could they ever practice?

Only upon reaching the Western Pure Land will you see that it is the person of suffering who gains the advantage, while the person of pleasure suffers a loss. Furthermore, observe those who do not believe in cultivation.
One who acts thus undergoes a lifetime of hardship, creating countless evil karmas. Before King Yama, one must suffer infinite retributions for these deeds.
What are these afflictions? Even if one possesses good karma, it merely allows for the enjoyment of fortunate rewards.
Yet, while enjoying such rewards, if one has created evil karma, before long one will likewise face suffering before King Yama. Even if one has no evil karma, how can one know the end of heaven?

When the merit of the immortals is exhausted, they must inevitably fall. Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha with sincerity and earnestness will, in this very life, rely upon the power of the Buddha to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, where they shall never again suffer the pains of saṃsāra. From the sea of suffering to ultimate bliss.
How far apart are they? All of these were spoken from the golden mouth of Śākyamuni Buddha. I now transmit the Buddha’s words to inform all people;
every single character is true speech and authentic speech. If there be anything untrue herein, may I forever fall into the Hell of Severed Tongues.
Regarding the work *Jingye zhijin* (The Ferry Crossing of Pure Deeds), which I previously composed for the laywoman Tang Zhen’nu:
its language is coarse and shallow, intended to make it easily understood. Nevertheless, when pursued to its ultimate depths, it does not transcend these principles.

These are merely shallow and mundane discourses; they most easily conform to worldly customs and are difficult to enter into the True Dharma of the Three Vehicles. Might this book perhaps be an exception?
When the lay practitioner Huang of Sichuan saw it, he rejoiced and subsequently donated funds to have it carved for printing.
This was in the third month of the Ji-chou year of the Daoguang era. Written by Wukai.
Regarding the "Shallow and Accessible Explanation of Rebirth through Nianfo," the term *namo* means "taking refuge. *Amitābha* means "Immeasurable Life. *Buddha* means "Awakened One.
This signifies that one should take refuge in the Honored One of Immeasurable Life and Great Awakening. Now, since there are many names for Buddhas, why should one focus exclusively on this one?
"Amitābha Buddha! Indeed, this is the Buddha within the minds of sentient beings. Observe those in the world: when they reach the height of joy, they cry out, "Amitābha Buddha!";
when they reach the height of suffering, they cry out, "Amitābha Buddha! This phrase of "Buddha" emerges spontaneously, without their being aware of it.
It flows forth naturally from the mouth; even the simple villagers, women, and children know it without being taught and are able to do so without learning.

Therefore, it is said that the mind is the Buddha. Because sentient beings have wandered through the cycle of rebirth for kalpas and lost their original nature, the Buddha opened the gate of extraordinary skillful means to teach people to contemplate themselves as their own Buddhas.
It is like a person in a dream who is awakened by calling out the single phrase "Amitābha."
If one loses mindfulness of these matters, one may use a single phrase—Amitābha—to serve as a reminder.

This draws suffering sentient beings to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and transforms the five turbidities of this evil world into pavilions made of the seven precious gems. If one can truly seek birth in the Pure Land with every breath, [this will come to pass].
Direct your mind and every thought toward the Western Land. When your mindfulness reaches a state of pure proficiency, it will naturally succeed like water reaching a channel.
The wanderer shall return to his native home; the infant shall once more be cast into the arms of its compassionate mother. Transcending the three realms horizontally, one shall never again regress.
One shall dwell securely in the nine grades of rebirth, having prepared for this in advance. How joyful this is! You must by no means say, "My karmic evil is too heavy and I cannot go."
My merit is meager and I am unable to go; yet you must know that Amitābha has his original vows and will certainly not deceive anyone.
A horse leaping into a deep pool crosses over with a single bound; a sparrow crossing the great ocean soars beyond with a single flight.

To entertain even the slightest hesitation is to fall into a pit or drown in water—this is an established principle. It is like wishing to reach Beijing: first one prepares the necessary funds, and then one hires a boat or carriage.

Advance your journey day by day; travel early so that you may arrive early. If your provisions for the road are insufficient, or if you abandon your boat or carriage, or linger at inns, you will surely encounter obstructions along the way.
Furthermore, with gales and torrential rain, scorching heat and bitter cold, dark nights and muddy quagmires, and treading upon thorns at every step, it will be too late for regrets.
To recite the Buddha’s name abundantly today is itself the provision for your journey to rebirth.
The Great Vow Boat of Amitābha is the compassionate vessel across the ocean of suffering. The clear revelation of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is like a south-pointing chariot.
To recite the Buddha’s name without seeking rebirth there is merely to plant seeds of wholesome causes, resulting perhaps only in worldly blessings.
Once these blessings are exhausted, one returns once more to the cycle of saṃsāra—how perilous! How terrifying!
Regarding the further explanation of the practice of *nienfo*:
I previously presented the "Shallow Discourse on Rebirth through *Nienfo*," which was intended to inspire faith in people and strengthen their aspirational power.
Now that the mind has been inspired and the vow has been strengthened, those who do not apply themselves with courageous diligence will find that the urgency of birth and death remains unaddressed.
Furthermore, the reason why birth and death do not strike one as urgent is that one does not yet know the suffering of saṃsāra, nor that reciting the Buddha’s name can lead one out of saṃsāra.

Please provide a further explanation. Now, such phrases as "the mind is itself the Buddha," "the Buddha is in the heart," and "the Pure Land is within the mind" are the most supreme, the most exalted, and the very first;
it is a pity that they are easily glossed over with idle speech and become mere empty words.
This is the primary Chan [teaching]. What the world calls the "mind" is merely a lump of flesh within the physical frame.
The eyes have discrimination because of forms; the ears have discrimination because of sounds. This deluded mind cannot exist apart from the six sense-objects.
When the four great elements disintegrate, it ultimately returns to dispersion and extinction. The *Platform Sutra* says: "The mind is the land; the nature is the king. The king—
Abiding upon the ground of the mind, if one speaks of its essence, it is formless and signless, without movement or fluctuation, neither arising nor ceasing.
If one speaks of its function, it can contain all things and give birth to all things; it is perfectly complete and pervasive, its operation inexhaustible.

Whether good or evil, perverse or correct, there is nothing it does not fully possess. A single thought of goodness leads to ascent to heaven; a single thought of evil leads to descent into hell. And yet...

If one contemplates Amitābha in every thought-moment and directs the mind toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss in every heart-moment, how could there be anyone who does not achieve success through this?
As goodness accumulates day by day, heaven rises layer upon layer; as evil accumulates day by day, hell descends layer upon layer.

The realms of the Pure Land are likewise differentiated according to the level of an individual’s cultivation and realization. Therefore, [the distinctions between] the east, west, south, and north...

The North is entirely the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*); even pagodas, temples, mountains, and forests are lands of bliss. Even if the golden platform comes to welcome one, it is likewise a manifestation within one's own nature.
In the heavens there is but a single moon, yet it is reflected everywhere—in lakes, seas, ditches, and channels, down to a single bowl or a single cup.
Only when the water is not clear does the moon fail to appear; this is a metaphor for when the minds of sentient beings are not pure.
One sees the Buddha. Indeed, one attains rebirth there. Seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one is liberated from the cycle of saṃsāra.

Someone asked: "When reciting the Buddha’s name, distracting thoughts are many; what should be done about this? He replied: "All thoughts are essentially empty and illusory. Nevertheless, they do not depart from the self-nature (svabhāva).
The Heart Sūtra states that the five aggregates are all empty. Clearly, there is a witness-presence. This is none other than the master who is neither distracted nor confused."

This is the old man’s view. He must say that the arising of thoughts hinders the recitation of the Buddha’s name. But if one asks, "Who is it that knows thoughts arise?"—knowing thoughts is itself detachment; detachment from thoughts is itself the Buddha.
Clinging to external objects is certainly wrong, yet suppressing and extinguishing thoughts is also a sickness. Let others give rise to their own thoughts, and I shall recite my own Buddha-name.
At first, the power of karma will prevail over the power of the Buddha; in time, the power of the Buddha will prevail over the power of karma. When [the practice] becomes pure, then...
Whether the mouth is open or closed, there remains nothing but the single phrase "Buddha. When it comes to that final sound at the end, it stops abruptly with a *ga-ra* resonance.
At this moment, all myriad thoughts vanish and all clamor falls silent. How refreshing! How much enjoyment!
In a single *kṣaṇa*, the stars shift and things change. Speaking from this perspective, human life—from youth, to maturity, to old age—is all...
This momentary experience of cool serenity cannot be attained.

Amidst the turmoil of worldly afflictions, one does not realize how much of one's innate truth has been lost in confusion, how much of one's spiritual nature has been buried, and how much of one's precious time has been wasted, leading to the cycle of birth and death.
When one reflects upon this, a sense of alarm arises and a feeling of trepidation awakens; seeking only to transcend birth and death, there is—
This path—reciting it aloud or silently, morning and evening—one cannot bear to cease. Nevertheless, this teaching of mine approaches the state of detachment from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
This teaching of detachment from characteristics is precisely the teaching for advancing toward a single understanding; yet, one cannot truly detach from characteristics.
This is still to be attached to signs. If one recognizes a dull, pitch-black void or a rigid, stagnant state of meditative absorption, that is a great error.
One must observe the precept against killing when reciting the Buddha’s name.

Reciting the Buddha’s name does not depend on whether one consumes meat or observes a vegetarian diet; it is originally the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas’ earnest effort to save the world, opening this gateway of expedient means (*upāya*).
People of the world have misunderstood this intent, and thus there are those who recite the Buddha’s name yet do not refrain from killing.

They fail to realize that among the three types of karma (*trividha-karma*), killing is foremost, and among the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), the prohibition against killing is the first. If one does not refrain from killing, one will inevitably bring about [karmic] retribution.

The continuity of karmic results obstructs rebirth in higher realms. Yuan Zhonglang said: "There has never been one who could attain purity and peace without first opening their mouth to the 'crane-knife' [of sincere repentance].
Indeed, all sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, possess Buddha-nature. Yet, due to delusion, they commit evil and transmigrate through the various realms of existence.
Through the compassionate power of his vows, the World-Honored One causes them to enter *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and attain liberation. It is the Buddha who delivers them.
Yet people kill them. What kind of mind is this? To kill those who serve the Buddha is the height of perversity and contradiction.
Some may say, "We do this for sacrifices, for daily sustenance, or to entertain guests. But consider this:

when a person serves the Way, there is none who does not wish that their ancestors and kinsmen may all ascend together through the nine grades and become fellow practitioners among the supreme sages. How can you suppress such a thought?
They gather together in one place; moved by compassion, they transform them, thereby delivering themselves and delivering others as well. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"If one kills their lives or eats their flesh, for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they will devour and slaughter one another without respite.

Thus we know that the abundance of animal species is entirely due to the retribution of the karma of killing. Humans are also included among these twelve classes of beings; I, therefore, cherish [them].

Fearing the suffering of life and death, one further desires to seek rebirth in a Pure Land. Yet, sentient beings are bound by fetters and ensnared by nets, ultimately ending up before the butcher’s blade.
When weighing the facts and deliberating the principles, this seems profoundly unjust.
As the ancient masters said: "The mouth is dripping with grease, yet the blade drips with blood; how can one bring it to the mouth? How can one bring it to the hand? May those of like mind take heed.
He repeated these words three times: "Not only shall you not kill them, but you shall purchase their release and further vow to deliver them all universally;
only then may you become a disciple of the Buddha. As for the minute details of living beings, one should cherish them; as for the ignorance of family members, one must guard against it.
This especially depends on those with a mindful heart, who should examine and observe at all times.
Jingye Zhijin (End): Disciple Jingtong.
Since birth after birth, I have transmigrated through birth and death with no foreseeable end to my suffering.

Now that I have encountered the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation, there is hope for liberation. I prostrate and pray that every person may possess courageous resolve for the Path and cultivate faith and aspiration.
May this be firm and steadfast. May we be born in peace and bliss in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

I pray with earnest longing that my parents of this life, as well as the parents and kinsmen of each individual, may be reborn together in the Lotus Realm and collectively realize Bodhi. I entreat the Buddha’s compassionate mercy to fulfill this vow of mine.
